label: Jupiter turning: the approach movie
why: Two days of narrow-angle frames as Jupiter turns, the source of the famous approach movies of its bands and the Great Red Spot

label: Jupiter portrait mosaic
why: The color mosaic of the whole of Jupiter, the most detailed global portrait of the planet ever made

label: Saturn on approach
why: Approach movie in color and methane filters, seven weeks before arrival

label: Watching Saturn turn
why: An 18 hour 2x2 mosaic movie of Saturn's atmosphere in color, the first long weather watch from orbit

label: Fountains of Enceladus
why: Backlit jets spraying from the south pole: the pictures that showed Enceladus is active

label: In Saturn's Shadow
why: Saturn eclipsing the Sun, the rings lit from behind and Earth a dot inside them; the mission's most famous mosaic

label: A day of Saturn's storms
why: Nearly a full day of storm-alley movie frames in color, Saturn turning beneath the camera

label: Daphnis makes waves at equinox
why: Near equinox the low Sun makes the waves Daphnis raises on the Keeler gap edge cast long shadows across the rings

label: Equinox mosaic
why: A wide-angle mosaic of the rings and planet the day after equinox, the rings nearly dark with the Sun edge-on

label: The Great Northern Storm
why: A high-resolution global map while the great storm of 2010-2011 wrapped around the planet

label: The Rose: north polar vortex
why: Close look into the hurricane at Saturn's north pole, the eye about 2000 km across

label: The hexagon from above
why: Eleven hours mapping the north pole and its hexagon jet stream in color, the best scored Saturn session in the archive

label: A day over the hexagon
why: Sixteen hours of wide-angle movie frames of the hexagon turning, the longest polar movie of the mission

label: The Day the Earth Smiled
why: Saturn backlit by the Sun with Earth a pale dot below the rings, while people on Earth waved

label: Saturn from above
why: From high above the north pole: the whole planet and its rings in one color mosaic, the shadow falling across the rings

label: Saturn's equator in color
why: Thirteen hours mapping the equatorial belts in color

label: Ring-grazing orbits begin
why: Polar movie on the first of the ring-grazing orbits that skimmed the outer edge of the main rings

label: Daphnis up close
why: The closest look at Daphnis, its ridge and the waves it raises in the Keeler gap

label: Pan up close
why: The ravioli-shaped moon Pan from about 22,000 km, its equatorial ridge built from ring material

label: Inside the gap: first dive
why: An hour of the closest pictures of Saturn's clouds ever taken, on the first dive between planet and rings

label: Earth through the rings
why: Looking back at the Sun through the rings from the Grand Finale orbit, Earth a bright point beneath them

label: The southern hemisphere in color
why: Twelve hours mapping the south in color from the Grand Finale orbits, a last full look at the planet

label: Titan's goodbye kiss
why: The last distant Titan flyby, which bent Cassini's orbit into the final plunge

label: Farewell mosaic
why: Cassini's last wide-angle color mosaic of Saturn and its rings

label: Enceladus sets behind Saturn
why: Enceladus, the moon that changed the mission, slipping behind Saturn's limb

label: The last pictures
why: The final images, of the spot where Cassini would enter the atmosphere the next day

label: Opposition spot on the rings
why: The point exactly opposite the Sun falls on the rings: a bright glow, the opposition surge, slides across them from frame to frame

label: Enceladus over edge-on rings
why: Close past Enceladus with Cassini almost exactly in the ring plane, so the rings are a thin line behind the moon

label: The young Great Storm, rings edge-on
why: Three weeks after the 2010 northern storm broke out: the rings seen edge-on as a thin line, the storm's bright head on the disc

label: The F ring turning
why: A steady 14-hour movie of the F ring, 1,334 frames every 37 seconds, with Prometheus and Pandora passing by

label: Spokes forming in the B ring
why: The densest burst of pictures in the mission, 55 frames every 10 minutes for five hours, watching ghostly spokes form in the B ring

label: Watching for spokes, 2008
why: Another six-hour spoke watch at the same dense cadence, 1,800 narrow-angle frames of the B ring

label: Saturn's shadow cuts the rings
why: Saturn's shadow lies across the rings as a sharp-edged dark band, seen from high above the ring plane

label: Backlit rings through the night side
why: From inside Saturn's shadow the rings glow with forward-scattered sunlight, crossed by the planet's dark limb

label: Eclipse ring scan
why: A pass through Saturn's shadow five months before the Earth-Smiled mosaic, the rings lit from behind

label: Rhea up close
why: The closest imaging pass of Rhea, about 6,600 km: crescent views, then cratered terrain at around 40 m per pixel

label: Rhea from over its pole
why: Cassini looks almost straight down on Rhea's pole, from 87 degrees latitude

label: First close Enceladus flyby
why: The first high-resolution look at Enceladus, from 4,300 km: a young, cracked and folded surface

label: Enceladus' tiger stripes up close
why: A day at Enceladus ending 2,900 km above the ridged south-polar terrain, the source of its jets, at about 20 m per pixel

label: First close look at Iapetus
why: New Year's Eve 2004: the first close views of Iapetus, its dark leading side and the equatorial ridge on the limb

label: Iapetus half-lit
why: Iapetus half in sunlight, its bright and dark terrains side by side along the terminator

label: Titan's ring of light, 2005
why: Leaving Titan at 160 degrees phase: its haze lit from behind as a complete bright ring around the dark moon

label: Hunting lightning on the night side
why: Fourteen hours staring at Saturn's dark side, 2,074 frames every 24 seconds, looking for flashes of lightning

label: Rings from 75 degrees above
why: On the steeply inclined 2008 orbits Cassini scans the rings looking almost straight down on them
